passage: Kunal was two and a half when he threw his cup, shoved his plate away and wailed at everything, even the toy he had asked for. His mother Preeti looked at the clock. Lunch was an hour late. She sat him down with warm rice and dal, and he ate in silence, sniffing. Ten minutes later he was laughing at a spoon. At fifteen, Kunal came home after a long practice snapping at everyone. His sister Rajni asked how his day went and he glared at her. Then he stopped and said, "Sorry. Let me eat something first, then we talk." He made two chapattis, ate them at the counter, and afterwards told her about the match. At twenty-five, Kunal skipped lunch to finish a report. By four o'clock he had typed a curt email to a colleague and read his own draft with cold certainty that his job was going nowhere. He texted Rajni, "Nothing I do here matters." She replied with a single line: "Have you eaten today? 🙂" He looked at the empty lunch box on his desk and went to the canteen.

qa.q: What did Kunal say to his sister after his practice at fifteen?
qa.a: He said, "Sorry. Let me eat something first, then we talk."

qa.q: How do Kunal's moods at two and a half, fifteen and twenty-five connect to food?
qa.a: At two and a half he threw his cup and wailed because lunch was an hour late, at fifteen he snapped after practice until he ate, and at twenty-five skipping lunch made a report feel hopeless and his email curt. Each time he calmed once he ate, though only at fifteen did he notice the pattern himself.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he texted Rajni that nothing he did there mattered?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and discouraged, and his empty stomach made the work look bigger and worse than it was. 😔

qa.q: What could Kunal do at work to avoid skipping meals when a deadline is close?
qa.a: He could set a time to eat before he starts on the report and keep a snack at his desk, so a low mood does not decide his emails.

grounding: The same person's mood tracks low fuel at three ages: a hungry toddler's tantrum, a teenager who learns to eat before talking, and an adult whose skipped lunch turns a report hopeless.

passage: At five, Kiran knelt on the doorstep with her little sister Devika's shoe and held the laces up. "Bunny ears first," she said, guiding the small fingers. When Devika finally made a bow, Kiran clapped louder than anyone. At twenty, she spent Saturday mornings at a community centre, helping schoolchildren with fractions. The centre's coordinator Jaya thanked her, and Kiran said, "I'd do it without the certificate." She hoped some of those children would remember the way they finally understood. She still wanted a good job and had applications out. At twenty-five, Kiran had a comfortable post, a steady pay slip and a regular lift home. Her evenings settled into the same shape: tea, a series, sleep. One weekend Jaya, who had become a friend, asked over coffee, "So what are you building these days?" Kiran opened her mouth, then reached for her cup. "Savings, I suppose." The answer felt thin as she said it. On the ride home she thought of the fractions morning and the wobbling bow, and could not say why they came to mind.

qa.q: What did Kiran help schoolchildren with at the community centre?
qa.a: She spent Saturday mornings helping schoolchildren with fractions.

qa.q: How does Kiran's wish to pass something on change from five to twenty to twenty-five?
qa.a: At five she taught Devika to tie a bow and was proud, at twenty she gave Saturday mornings to schoolchildren wanting some of it to be remembered, and at twenty-five she has a comfortable routine but only savings to show when asked what she is building. The urge to pass something on faded into a life turned inward.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when she answered "Savings, I suppose."?
qa.a: She felt flat and a bit dissatisfied, since the answer sounded thin to her, and she was unsure why.

qa.q: What small step could Kiran take to reconnect with what she liked about teaching?
qa.a: She could return to the community centre for a morning or teach someone a skill she has, without any certificate or credit.

grounding: One person's generative urge shows at five as teaching a sibling, at twenty as mentoring, and at twenty-five as a settled routine that feels flat when asked what she is building.

passage: Yusuf, ten, slammed his bedroom door and shouted that it was unfair. His mother Rukmini shouted back, louder, and heard her own voice bouncing off the walls. The more she raised it, the more he screamed. Then she stopped, took a breath, and sat on the stairs. In a low voice she said, "I'm going to sit here until we both feel calmer." Ten minutes later the door opened a crack. They talked about the homework, quietly. Ten years on, Yusuf was in the hostel common room when a wing-mate, Urmila, burst in and shouted that he had told a lie about her to the warden. Her face was red, her voice sharp, and his heart pounded. He wanted to shout back. He thought of the stairs and his mother's low voice. He stepped back, kept the table between them, and said quietly, "I hear you're angry. I'll talk when we both can." Urmila glared, then her shoulders dropped. "I'm sorry," she muttered. "I was wrong about what I heard."

qa.q: Where did Rukmini sit after she stopped shouting?
qa.a: She sat on the stairs.

qa.q: What do Rukmini's response on the stairs and Yusuf's response to Urmila have in common?
qa.a: Both refused to match the volume of the person shouting: Rukmini lowered her voice and paused, and Yusuf stepped back, kept the table between them and spoke quietly. In both cases the other person's storm eased and they could talk when calm.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when Urmila shouted at him in the common room?
qa.a: He felt shocked and afraid, with his heart pounding and a wish to shout back.

qa.q: What could Urmila do next after realising she was wrong about what she heard?
qa.a: She could apologise properly to Yusuf and check the facts before she confronts someone.

grounding: Two people on the receiving end of shouting: a parent who first escalates then calms and lowers her voice, and her son years later, who keeps distance and does not match a hostel argument's volume.

passage: Bhavna, nine, stood at the pool's edge with her stomach fluttering. "This place is dangerous," she told her mother Mehak. "I can feel it." The lifeguard was standing right there and the water was shallow, but the flutter felt like proof. At fifteen, she got twenty-two out of fifty in a chemistry test and felt heavy all evening. "I'm useless," she told the ceiling. "I always was." She told her mother at dinner, and Mehak sat beside her and said, "That sounds like a heavy feeling. A bad test is one test." Together they wrote down the topics she had missed, and Mehak phoned the teacher next morning to ask for help. At twenty, Bhavna's friend Harsha went quiet at the canteen and stared at his tea. She thought, I must have hurt him, I feel so guilty. She did not sleep. The next day she asked, "Is it something I did?" Harsha looked surprised. "No! My interview is on Monday and I'm so nervous." She let out a long breath, still glad she had asked.

qa.q: How many marks did Bhavna get in her chemistry test?
qa.a: She got twenty-two out of fifty.

qa.q: What does Bhavna do with her feelings at nine, fifteen and twenty?
qa.a: At nine she treated her nervousness as proof that the pool was dangerous, at fifteen she took her heavy mood after the test as proof she was useless, and at twenty she took her guilt as proof she had hurt Harsha. Each time the feeling was real but was not evidence, as shown by the lifeguard, the missed topics and Harsha's interview.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when Harsha went quiet at the canteen?
qa.a: She felt guilty and worried that she had hurt him, which kept her awake all night.

qa.q: How could Mehak support Bhavna after the chemistry test?
qa.a: She could listen, name the feeling, help sort out what was missed and speak to the teacher, as she did the next morning.

grounding: The same person treats a strong feeling as a fact about the world at nine, about herself at fifteen, and about her own guilt at twenty.

passage: Gopika, the elderly neighbour whom Dilnaz visited on Sunday afternoons, began again on the story of the train that arrived at midnight with all her wedding luggage lost. Dilnaz had heard it many times. She poured the tea, settled into the cane chair, and this time asked, "What did you do first when you saw the platform was empty?" Gopika lit up. "I sat on my trunk and sang!" Her eyes shone, and she went on for an hour while Dilnaz simply listened. Four years later, Gopika got a new phone and called in a fluster. Dilnaz's cousin Devika, visiting, muttered, "She'll never learn." Dilnaz ignored her. She placed the phone in Gopika's hands and said slowly, "Touch the green circle. That's the one. Now the name." She waited while Gopika pressed it herself. When the video call opened on her granddaughter's face, Gopika gasped and clapped. Later, Dilnaz read out the doctor's paper line by line, letting Gopika repeat each one back in her own words.

qa.q: What did Gopika sing when she sat on her trunk?
qa.a: She said she sat on her trunk and sang.

qa.q: How do Dilnaz's ways of being with Gopika at twenty and at twenty-four differ and what do they share?
qa.a: At twenty she let the old story be told again and asked a new question about it, and at twenty-four she explained the phone and the doctor's paper slowly and let Gopika press the buttons herself. Both times she was patient and preserved Gopika's dignity instead of hurrying her or teasing.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when the video call opened on her granddaughter's face?
qa.a: She felt delighted and proud that she had done it herself, which is why she gasped and clapped.

qa.q: What could Devika do differently after seeing how Dilnaz helped Gopika?
qa.a: She could slow down, explain without teasing, and let Gopika do the steps herself.

grounding: The same person treats an elder with patience: listening to a familiar story with a fresh question, then explaining technology and health information slowly while the elder does the steps.

passage: "Mm-hmm," said Gautam, eyes on his phone, when his mother Kalyani asked whether he had finished his homework. She paused with the ladle in her hand. It could mean yes, or it could mean leave me alone. "Was that a yes, or a brush-off? Tell me in words." Gautam looked up, half smiling. "Brush-off. But also yes. Almost." He put the phone down and opened his notebook. At twenty, Gautam messaged his hostel-mate Arnab that he had got a summer internship. The reply arrived a minute later: "wow." No emoji, no full stop after it, nothing more. Gautam read it four times. Was Arnab impressed? Envious? Making fun? He could not tell, and his pleasure drained away. He typed "?" and got no reply, so he rang. Arnab picked up from a noisy bus. "I was typing with one hand, yaar! Wow means wow. That's amazing, honestly." Gautam grinned and felt silly. "Next time write more than three letters," he said, and they both laughed.

qa.q: What did Gautam say when his mother asked about his homework?
qa.a: He said, "Mm-hmm."

qa.q: How are Gautam's "mm-hmm" and Arnab's "wow" alike, and how does each get cleared up?
qa.a: Both short sounds could mean different things, the mm-hmm a yes or a brush-off and the wow admiration, envy or sarcasm, because tone and voice were missing. Kalyani asked in words and Gautam rang Arnab, and each follow-up settled the meaning.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling as he read Arnab's one-word reply four times?
qa.a: He felt uncertain and a little hurt, as his pleasure drained away when he could not tell whether Arnab was impressed or mocking.

qa.q: What could Arnab do next time Arnab replies to good news by message?
qa.a: Arnab could add a few more words or an emoji so the warmth comes through, or call when not typing on a bus.

grounding: The same person meets ambiguous short sounds at two ages: a spoken mm-hmm from a teenager and a one-word wow in a text, each settled by a follow-up question or call.
